options.text: int read() { return get(); }  goes through the inherited accessor instead of naming the field.
int read() { return v; }  reads the field by name, which is what the field being private forbids.

options.text: int read() { return this.v; }  qualifies the name with this, which reaches the inherited copy.

options.text: int read() { return get() + 1; }  calls the accessor but adjusts the value on the way out.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Claims about an override that drops synchronized
questions.learningObjective: judge what happens to mutual exclusion when an override is not synchronized
questions.stem: A superclass method is declared synchronized and a subclass overrides the same signature without the modifier. A cheat sheet lists four claims about the result. Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The override gives no mutual exclusion, because the lock is taken only by synchronized methods.
A thread inside the override can run at the same time as a thread inside the base method.
The compiler rejects the override, since a synchronized method may not be overridden loosely.
options.misconception: believes the compiler enforces synchronized on overrides

options.text: The inherited synchronized modifier still applies, because modifiers travel with an overridden method.
options.misconception: believes modifiers are inherited along with the method

questions.explanation: The rule is that a synchronized method acquires the monitor of its object for the duration of the call, and that behaviour belongs to the individual method body rather than to the signature, so an override that omits the modifier simply runs without holding the lock. The two claims that are false both assume some form of automatic protection: the compiler enforcing the modifier, or the modifier travelling down the hierarchy with the method. Neither happens, which is why an override that drops synchronized is a genuine and quiet bug rather than a rejected program.
questions.hint: The lock is a property of a method body, not of a signature.

questions.topic: A subclass that never implements the abstract operation

options.text: static class Circle extends Shape { String label() { return "circle"; } }  implements the step, so the class is concrete.
static class Circle extends Shape { }  inherits the abstract step, leaving the class abstract at the call.
options.misconception: believes an unimplemented step is inherited as a body

options.text: static abstract class Circle extends Shape { }  stays abstract deliberately, so the call must still work.

options.text: static class Circle extends Shape { private String label() { return "circle"; } }  keeps the step private to the subclass.

The compiler's complaint about the original line is that Circle is not abstract and does not override the abstract method, which is a specific error rather than a vague one. Option C is the answer that looks like a fix, since marking the subclass abstract removes the inconsistency, but it moves the failure to the new expression instead of solving it.
questions.hint: The class has to be concrete at the point where it is instantiated.

questions.topic: One template calling two hook implementations

[B][s] - the abstract declaration decides the text, so the classes run in reverse order.

questions.topic: A static call written inside an inherited instance method
questions.learningObjective: predict that a static helper call is bound where the method body lives

options.text: 11 - the call is bound in A, where the body was written, so the hiding version in B is unused.
15 - the runtime class supplies the helper, so B's bonus of 5 is the one added.
options.misconception: believes a static call dispatches on the runtime class

options.text: 10 - a hidden static method is not callable from the base class at all, so the term vanishes.
options.misconception: believes hiding makes the base method uncallable

options.text: 5 - the inherited total() is replaced by the subclass's static helper of the same name.
options.misconception: believes a static method overrides an inherited instance method

questions.explanation: The rule is that a static call inside a method body is resolved at compile time using the class whose source contains the body, so total() is written in A and unqualified bonus() means A.bonus, giving 10 + 1. The object happens to be a B, but static calls are precisely the case where the runtime class is irrelevant, and B.bonus hides rather than overrides, so it is simply never consulted here. The answer 15 is the single most common wrong reading in this area, because dynamic dispatch is such a strong habit that applying it to a static call feels like correctness.
questions.hint: Static calls are decided by where they are written, not by the object.

B then caught no - the subclass body runs first, and the superclass throws afterwards.
